content: The concept of acceptability in medical interventions refers to the degree of convenience and satisfaction perceived by patients regarding the treatment and services provided. It also encompasses the extent to which healthcare providers and program managers consider a screening test or treatment intervention to be appropriate. Definitions of acceptability may vary depending on the authors or context. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: Higher acceptability can lead to improved compliance with future screening and treatment, greater community acceptance, and enhanced delivery of screening and treatment interventions. Assessment: Visual scales are often employed for this purpose. Thresholds: Scales may be categorized into acceptable or not acceptable. Treatment: Not applicable. Time Horizon: Acceptability can be assessed immediately after treatment or during follow-up visits. Screening Test Performance 1. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV of a screening test to detect high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+), cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+), or grade 3 or higher (CIN3+) is often reported in screen-and-treat studies. These studies typically focus on women who test positive during screening. Some studies may include cervical biopsies before administering ablative treatment, allowing for an estimation of the PPV of the screening test. The PPV is calculated as the number of histopathologically confirmed high-grade lesions (e.g., HSIL-CIN2, HSIL-CIN3, adenocarcinoma in situ [AIS]) divided by the total number of women who tested positive and had satisfactory histopathology results, multiplied by 100. The PPV is directly related to the risk of overtreatment. 2. Overtreatment Rate: This is defined as the number of women treated without any CIN or AIS detected on histopathology after treatment, divided by the total number of treated women with available histopathology results, multiplied by 100. 3. Sensitivity, Specificity, and Negative Predictive Value (NPV): These accuracy statistics are rarely reported in screen-and-treat studies because screen-negative populations are not typically evaluated further. However, it is ideal to provide sensitivity, specificity, and NPV when possible. 4. Reduction in Cervical Cancer Incidence: This refers to the decrease in the rate of newly diagnosed cervical cancer cases in a population over a defined time period. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: Not applicable. Assessment: New cancer cases are histopathologically diagnosed through active follow-up or linkage to screening and cancer registries. Thresholds: Not applicable. Time Horizon: A reduction in incidence may be observed over 5–10 years. 5. Reduction in Cervical Cancer Mortality: This refers to the decrease in the rate of deaths from cervical cancer following treatment within a defined time period. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: Not applicable. Assessment: Mortality reduction is assessed through linkage with population-based cancer registries or mortality databases and active follow-up. Thresholds: Not applicable. Time Horizon: Mortality reduction may be observed over 5–10 years. 6. Unnecessary Interventions or Overtreatment: Each round of screening may result in unnecessary interventions, such as colposcopy and biopsy, for women with false-positive results, as well as overtreatment of lesions that may not progress. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: These include side effects and complications from biopsy and treatment, psychological harm, and resource implications. Assessment: This is estimated based on the false-positive rate of the screening test and colposcopy, as well as progression rates of different CIN grades from natural history studies. Thresholds: Not applicable. Time Horizon: Depends on the screening interval. Treatment Coverage and Rates 1. Treatment Coverage: This is the proportion of eligible women treated in a population. It is calculated as the number of women completing treatment within a defined time frame divided by the total number of screen-positive women eligible for treatment in the same time frame, multiplied by 100. The time frame is usually no more than 12 months. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: Low treatment coverage increases the risk of invasive cancer and mortality and reduces the impact of the screening program on cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Assessment: Data is collected through information systems or screening registries with linkage between screening and treatment services. Thresholds: None; higher values indicate better impact. Time Horizon: 12 months. 2. Treatment Rate: This is the proportion of eligible women treated in a study, calculated as the number of treated women divided by the number of eligible women. Symptoms: Not applicable. Consequences: Higher treatment rates improve the likelihood of achieving the desired impact on cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Assessment: Data is recorded during the study. Thresholds: Not applicable. Treatment: Includes cryotherapy, thermal ablation, large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), or referral. Time Horizon: Duration of the study. Treatment Interventions 1. Therapeutic Intervention: This involves treating a diagnosed cervical lesion with the intent to completely remove the transformation zone through ablation or excision, provided there are no contraindications. 2. Diagnostic Intervention: This involves obtaining additional tissue for analysis to guide further therapy. Cervical Anatomy for Treatment The transformation zone (TZ) is the region of the cervix where columnar epithelium has been replaced or is being replaced by metaplastic squamous epithelium. The visibility and position of the TZ are categorized as: Type 1: Entirely visible and ectocervical. Type 2: Entirely visible with an endocervical component. Type 3: Not entirely visible, extending into the endocervical canal. Methods of Treatment for Preinvasive Cervical Disease 1. LLETZ (Large-Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone): This excisional method uses a wire loop electrode to remove the transformation zone and lesion, ensuring a disease-free margin of at least 2–3 mm. It is used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. 2. Thermal Ablation: This involves destroying abnormal cervical tissue using extreme heat (≥100°C). 3. Cryotherapy: This involves applying extreme cold to the cervix using a cryoprobe to freeze abnormal areas. 4. Cold Knife Conization (CKC): This surgical procedure removes the central cervix, including portions of the ectocervix and endocervix, using a scalpel. It is typically performed under anesthesia in a hospital. Screening and Diagnostic Tools 1. Self-Collected Samples: Women can collect vaginal samples for high-risk HPV DNA testing using kits with swabs or brushes. This method is discreet, private, and time-saving, overcoming cultural and logistical barriers to accessing healthcare. 2. HPV Tests: These tests detect high-risk HPV genotypes, particularly types 16 and 18, which are associated with the highest risk of cervical cancer. Molecular testing identifies HPV DNA in vaginal or cervical samples. 3. Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA): VIA involves applying a 3–5% acetic acid solution to the cervix to identify acetowhite lesions, which may indicate CIN2/3 or invasive cancer. It is most effective in women under 50 years of age with a visible transformation zone. 4. Cytology (Pap Smear): This test examines cervical cells for abnormalities, such as atypical squamous cells of uncertain significance (ASCUS) or lowto high-grade changes, which may indicate precancerous conditions. 5. Colposcopy: A colposcope is used to visually assess the cervix and determine the transformation zone type and grade of epithelial abnormality. It also facilitates biopsy and excisional treatment. 6. Histology: The diagnosis of CIN is confirmed through histopathological examination of tissue obtained via biopsy, endocervical curettage, or excision.
